title: Harishchandra's Promise
hookLine: a king keeps his word, and his family pays too
carry: satya: truth, honored, with its cost in view
tomorrow: why can't two betrayed men stop worrying about who betrayed them?
last: THE HARD AGE HAS THE LOW DOOR.

lines: THE CAR IS DEAD. THE PROMISE ISN'T.
A GIFT, AND THE SAGE ASKS FOR ALL.
HE KEEPS IT. ALL OF IT.
cards: Somebody in a group chat promised to drive everyone to the concert. Now the car's dead and the only other one belongs to their mom, who needs it. Do they keep the promise whatever it costs, or call it off?
A small version of a very old argument. In the Markandeya Purana, a king named Harishchandra promises the sage Vishvamitra a gift, and the sage asks for everything. Harishchandra keeps the promise.
All of it. Readers have argued about him ever since.

teach.b: In the Markandeya Purana, the king hands over his kingdom. The sage demands a further fee.

To pay it, Harishchandra sells his wife Shaibya and their son Rohita into service, then sells himself to the keeper of a cremation ground. One day a grieving mother brings a boy who died of a snakebite.
It's Shaibya, with Rohita. Even then the king asks for the fee his master is owed. Then the gods appear, the boy lives, and all is restored.

teach.h: SATYA: THE KING WHO SPOKE TRUTH.
teach.b: The first is why Hindus still call him Satyavadi Harishchandra, the king who spoke truth. Satya, truth, is one of the foundations of dharma, and a king's word that can be bargained down isn't a word.

As a boy, Gandhi saw a play about Harishchandra, and wrote that it haunted him. Harishchandra doesn't make others pay to save himself; he pays first, and most, and at the end the gods themselves come to honor him.

The second view is in the Purana too. In the next chapter, the sage Vasishtha, the king's family priest, hears what was done and is furious at Vishvamitra. The two sages curse each other into enormous birds and fight.
Some readers hear in that rage the text admitting the cost was real, and they keep asking about Shaibya and Rohita, who never made the promise.
The Purana keeps both: the honored king, and the angry sage.

how: Harishchandra's story is retold in Hindu homes, plays and films as a story about truthfulness; the Markandeya Purana, which tells it, is also the home of the Devi Mahatmya.

o: a Purana told in the name of a long-lived sage
the law code that tells kings how to rule
a hymn praising Vishnu's ten descents to earth

games.q: who's who in Harishchandra's story — tap the pairs.
p: the king who kept his word
the sage who asked for everything
the sage furious at the cruelty
the wife and son who paid too

s: the Purana only praises Harishchandra; no one in it objects
in the next chapter Vasishtha is furious at what Vishvamitra did.
Harishchandra sold his family but kept himself free
he sold himself too, to the keeper of a cremation ground.
in the end the gods appear and Rohita lives
the story ends with the boy alive and the king honored.

games.q: your friend says Harishchandra was simply a terrible father. what's the strongest case for the other side?
o: he didn't think about his family; kings didn't, back then.
his word was the ground he stood on, and he paid first and most himself.
he knew all along the gods would put everything right.
games.why: the truth view at its best: he never made others pay to spare himself. and the other view is in the text too: Vasishtha's anger.

practice: Bring to mind one promise you've made that has started to feel heavy. Name what you hoped it would do, then what's in the way, then the true next step, whether that's keeping it or telling the person the honest truth.
If you pray, offer that step to God. Breathe slowly with it until the bell.

wordCard.voice: The Markandeya. The Purana told in the sage Markandeya's name, and inside it, Harishchandra, the king who kept his word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: truth, what is real. Harishchandra's story is told as a story about satya.

carryVoice: Your line: satya, truth, honored, with its cost in view. An honored king and an angry sage, kept side by side. That's today.
